content: The Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) is a temporary family planning method that leverages the natural effects of breastfeeding on fertility. Lactational refers to breastfeeding, and amenorrhea means the absence of monthly bleeding. For LAM to be effective, three conditions must be met: the mother’s monthly bleeding has not returned, the baby is exclusively or nearly exclusively breastfed frequently day and night, and the baby is less than six months old. Exclusive breastfeeding means the infant receives only breast milk, with no other liquids or foods, not even water. Nearly exclusive breastfeeding allows for occasional supplementation with vitamins, water, or other nutrients, but the majority of feeds must still be breast milk. LAM works by suppressing ovulation through the hormonal effects of frequent breastfeeding. The effectiveness of LAM depends on proper use. When used correctly, fewer than 1 in 100 women relying on LAM in the first six months postpartum will become pregnant. However, as commonly practiced, about 2 pregnancies per 100 women occur during this period. Fertility returns once LAM is discontinued, depending on how much the woman continues to breastfeed. LAM does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Women with certain conditions, such as HIV infection, or those taking specific medications, may need to consider alternative contraceptive methods. Additionally, LAM may not be suitable if the baby has conditions that make breastfeeding difficult, such as prematurity or oral deformities. To use LAM effectively, breastfeeding should occur on demand, at least 10–12 times daily in the first few weeks postpartum, and 8–10 times daily thereafter, including at least one nighttime feeding. Daytime feedings should not be more than four hours apart, and nighttime feedings should not exceed six hours apart. If the baby does not naturally breastfeed this frequently, gentle encouragement may be needed. Other foods should be introduced at six months, as breast milk alone will no longer fully meet the baby’s nutritional needs. LAM has no side effects and offers health benefits, including reduced risks associated with pregnancy and promotion of optimal breastfeeding patterns, which benefit both mother and baby. There are no known health risks associated with LAM. Women can switch to another contraceptive method at any time while using LAM, and if all three LAM criteria are still met, it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. If any of the LAM criteria are no longer met, another contraceptive method should be adopted immediately. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), also known as morning-after pills, prevent or delay ovulation and are ineffective if a woman is already pregnant. They can be taken up to five days after unprotected sex, but the sooner they are taken, the more effective they are. ECPs do not protect against STIs and are safe for all women, including those who cannot use ongoing hormonal contraceptives. Side effects may include slight irregular bleeding, nausea, abdominal pain, fatigue, headaches, breast tenderness, dizziness, or vomiting. If vomiting occurs within two hours of taking progestin-only or combined ECPs, or within three hours of taking ulipristal acetate ECPs, another dose should be taken. Routine use of anti-nausea medications is not recommended but may be used if needed. Fertility returns immediately after taking ECPs, so another contraceptive method should be started to prevent pregnancy from future acts of unprotected sex. Fertility awareness-based (FAB) methods involve identifying the fertile days of a woman’s menstrual cycle to avoid unprotected sex during this time. These methods include calendar-based approaches, such as the Standard Days Method, and symptoms-based methods, such as monitoring cervical secretions or basal body temperature (BBT). FAB methods require consistent and correct use to be effective. For example, the Standard Days Method is suitable for women with regular cycles lasting 26–32 days. Symptoms-based methods involve observing fertility signs, such as cervical secretions or a rise in BBT after ovulation. Couples can prevent pregnancy by abstaining from unprotected sex during fertile days or using barrier methods like condoms. FAB methods have no side effects or health risks but require proper training and commitment to use effectively. Male condoms are thin sheaths, typically made of latex, that fit over an erect penis to prevent pregnancy and protect against STIs. They are widely available and known by various names, such as rubbers or prophylactics.
